Title: Mexico Bans Violent Content on Social Media for Children

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/world/americas/mexico-media-bans-children.html

Published Time: 2026-10-14T23:11:42.000Z

Joining a global movement, President Claudia Sheinbaum signed a decree requiring the removal of a range of material for people under 18 and held out the prospect of tougher measures.

Listen

· 5:44 min

![Image 1: A hand reaches into a box filled with clear plastic bags holding phones.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/14/multimedia/14int-mexico-socialmedia01-photo-gfvk/14int-mexico-socialmedia01-photo-gfvk-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

A student turning over his phone before entering a classroom in Mexico City on Tuesday. Mexico has clamped down on phone use in schools.Credit...Marco Ugarte/Associated Press

Oct. 14, 2026 Updated 10:03 p.m. ET

Mexico banned violent and sexual content on social media for children and teenagers on Wednesday, joining a global movement on regulating technology but drawing questions about the government’s approach and legality.

President Claudia Sheinbaum signed a decree prohibiting digital platforms from allowing people under 18 to be exposed to or recommended content that “generates or promotes” a range of harmful behavior. That includes hate speech, extreme violence, abuse, sexual violence, suicide, deliberate self-harm, eating disorders, school violence, cyberbullying and sexually explicit material.

The decree will require social media companies to immediately remove content or accounts that promote violence and to verify users’ ages. They will have to offer parental supervision tools, provide mechanisms for reporting violent content and maintain a round-the-clock point of contact for the authorities. And they will be required to immediately alert the authorities when life-threatening content is spotted.

The decree won’t take effect for a month. Ms. Sheinbaum said that the social media companies “were in agreement” during meetings with the government but asked for time to adjust their platforms.

She also warned tech companies.

“We will be monitoring the situation,” said Ms. Sheinbaum, whose political party also controls the judiciary and legislature. “If it is not complied with, then we move to the next step, which is no longer just a presidential decree but a law. And if there is a law, then sanctions would follow.”

Image

![Image 2: The Mexican president standing outside.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/14/multimedia/14int-mexico-socialmedia02-photo-fgcb/14int-mexico-socialmedia02-photo-fgcb-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico in September.Credit...Cristopher Rogel Blanquet/Getty Images

Several of the social media companies named by the government — Google, TikTok, X and Apple — did not respond to requests for comment on Wednesday. Microsoft declined to comment.

In a statement, Meta said it had been working for years to give parents the ability to supervise their children online and to provide young users with accounts limiting what they see. “We share the president’s goal of a safer digital environment for teens in Mexico," the company said, “and will continue engaging with the government to support that work.”

Governments worldwide are [clamping down on tech companies](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/26/world/americas/children-social-media-restrictions-global-movement-meta.html) in hopes of shielding children from social media’s potential harms. [Australia](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/10/world/australia/australia-social-media-ban-under-16.html), [Britain](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/15/world/europe/uk-social-media-children.html) and [France](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/21/world/europe/france-social-media-ban.html) have adopted age verification laws as have several U.S. states.

Tech companies are challenging the state laws in court, arguing that they infringe on free speech rights. But some other countries do not have the same speech protections as the United States.

In late August, Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, [reached a landmark settlement](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/26/technology/meta-settlement-social-media-addiction-lawsuit.html) with 47 states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories, agreeing to pay up to $17.1 billion in penalties and make major changes to its products over claims that they endangered children.

In Mexico, some legislators have been [considering how](https://comunicacionsocial.senado.gob.mx/informacion/comunicados/16440-propone-alberto-anaya-impedir-que-menores-de-13-anos-utilicen-redes-sociales) to regulate children’s access to social media. Last month, the government [restricted cellphones and screens](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/22/world/americas/mexico-bans-phones-schools.html) in the country’s educational system.

Ms. Sheinbaum has said that the new decree is a response to an attack earlier this month at a secondary school in northern Mexico — rare in the country — in which two brothers who were former students killed an assistant principal and injured others. On Wednesday, she recounted another incident in which a child told a teacher that another student had talked of bringing a gun to the school.The authorities found a pistol in the child’s home, she said.

“In this instance,” she said, “as in other cases we have seen in Mexico, it was shown that the young people involved were communicating through digital platforms.”

José Merino, who serves in Ms. Sheinbaum’s cabinet as the head of Mexico’s digital transformation and telecommunications agency, said at a news conference last week that the decree would target publicly accessible content and its quick removal.

A legal adviser to Ms. Sheinbaum, Luisa María Alcalde, said Wednesday that the decree was based on an [existing law](https://www.diputados.gob.mx/LeyesBiblio/pdf/LGDNNA.pdf) guaranteeing Mexican children “safe access” to the internet but forbidding “cyberbullying and all forms of violence.”

She said that the government had held two meetings with tech company representatives and that they did not resist. They “fully understood the need,” she said.

But some digital rights experts have raised concerns about the government’s approach.

Vladimir Chorny, a researcher and legal expert with R3D, a Mexican digital rights group, said that the children’s law the government cited punished infractions but did not allow for censorship. The [Mexican Constitution](https://www.scjn.gob.mx/sites/default/files/pagina/documentos/2016-12/CONSTI%20INGLES%20SEPT%202010.pdf), he said, prohibits that. A judicial order is needed, he said, to remove content relating to child sexual abuse or incitement of violence.

Mr. Chorny said a better route would be to pass a law, after public debate, requiring social media companies to be more transparent about their algorithms and hold them accountable for their actions.

“We have to arrive at that answer collectively,” he said. “It’s not a decision to be made in a closed-door meeting, nor is it something that can simply be decreed.”

He said: “I believe the only way to truly protect children and adolescents is by strengthening their autonomy so they can distinguish which content affects them and which doesn’t. And the only way to achieve that is by tackling the addictive designs and business models of major platforms that exploit them for economic gain.”

Cecilia Kang contributed reporting,

[James Wagner](https://www.nytimes.com/by/james-wagner) covers news and culture in Latin America for The Times. He is based in Mexico City.

## Why Trump’s Diesel Deal With Putin Won’t Knock Down High Prices

President Trump’s deal with Russia will probably not lower diesel prices that have soared because of his war with Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries.

Oct. 14, 2026 Updated 5:25 p.m. ET

Diesel prices in the United States are hovering near record highs — and a deal President Trump announced last week to increase Russian fuel exports is unlikely to lower them significantly anytime soon.

The amount of diesel Russia could supply under that agreement is much lower than what the country was exporting this time last year and constitutes a small proportion of the diesel supply the world has lost because of Mr. Trump’s war with Iran, energy analysts said. And it is not clear that Russia could even deliver all the fuel the president and Russian offiicials have promised.

The numbers are stark.

From July through September of 2025, Russia exported around 693,000 barrels of diesel a day, according to S&P Global Energy. For the same period this year, the country exported around 140,000 barrels a day. Now, Mr. Trump and a Russian deputy prime minister, Alexander Novak, say that the country would export 300,000 metric tons of diesel in October, or roughly 75,000 barrels a day when stretched across a month.

The numbers under Mr. Trump’s deal with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia look even more meager when compared with the diesel that the world is no longer getting from the Middle East since the United States and Israel began attacking Iran on Feb. 28. Saudi Arabia and other countries in the Middle East exported 809,000 fewer barrels of diesel every day from July through the end of September, compared with the same period in 2025, according to S&P Global data.

“The main issue is still the Strait of Hormuz, that there is not enough diesel coming out of the Strait of Hormuz,” said Sarah Raffoul, oil product analyst at Argus, referring to the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which a significant share of the world’s fuels used to flow.

The shortfall of diesel supplies from the Middle East and Russia is the main reason the price of the fuel is up by around 77 percent so far this year.

The streamer’s share price is down more than 40 percent over the last year as the company has struggled with stalling engagement.

Listen

· 2:30 min

![Image 1: Netflix corporate offices in Los Angeles.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/14/multimedia/14biz-netflix-layoffs-1-lvzg/14biz-netflix-layoffs-1-lvzg-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

This is the company’s widest round of job cuts since 2022, when Netflix experienced a rare dip in subscriber figures.Credit...Mario Tama/Getty Images

Oct. 14, 2026 Updated 1:21 p.m. ET

Netflix announced Wednesday morning that it was laying off roughly 6 percent of its work force, or about 1,000 employees, as the company confronts slowing growth.

Most of the affected employees worked for the product, technology, legal and human resources teams, the company’s co-chief executives told employees in a memo.

“Our mission — to entertain the world — is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources,” Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters, the co-chief executives, wrote.

Mr. Sarandos and Mr. Peters also noted that “our business is strong and growing,” and that the company remains on track to deliver its full-year forecast.

Still, Netflix’s share price is down more than 40 percent over the last year as the company has struggled with stalling engagement. Recently, the company has pivoted in different directions, including signing up dozens of podcasters and creators from YouTube to help boost viewing time, particularly [during the daytime hours](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/23/business/media/youtube-has-a-firm-grip-on-daytime-tv.html).

A year ago, Netflix accounted for 8.8 percent of all television viewing time in the United States, compared with YouTube’s 13.4 percent, according to Nielsen. This year, Netflix’s figure has slipped to 7.8 percent while YouTube’s has increased to over 14 percent, Nielsen said.

“Overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” Mr. Sarandos said at a Bloomberg conference [this month.](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-01/sarandos-says-netflix-not-growing-as-fast-as-i-want)

Mr. Sarandos and Mr. Peters said on Wednesday that the company will “continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation.” A Netflix spokeswoman declined to comment beyond the memo.

This is the company’s widest round of job cuts [since 2022](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/05/17/business/netflix-layoffs.html), when Netflix experienced a rare dip in subscriber figures. Disney also announced a recent round of layoffs, and Skydance, the one-week-old company that brought together Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, is expected to undergo significant job cuts in the coming months as well.

[John Koblin](https://www.nytimes.com/by/john-koblin) covers the television industry for The Times.

# What Is Starshield, SpaceX’s Military-Grade Satellite Internet Service?

For years, Ukraine’s armed forces have relied on satellite communication services developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Recent restrictions have hampered its war effort.

[Audio 2](https://static.nytimes.com/narrated-articles/synthetic/article-5927b4e0-bfad-5a20-8dfc-bab287304735/job-1792016467707/article-5927b4e0-bfad-5a20-8dfc-bab287304735-job-1792016467707.mp3)

*   Share full article

*   371 

![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/14/multimedia/14Biz-Starshield-Explainer-gchj/14Biz-Starshield-Explainer-gchj-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

A Starlink dish camouflaged near the Eastern frontline in the Donetsk region of Ukraine in the summer of 2023.Credit...Sasha Maslov for The New York Times

[![Image 2: Ryan Mac](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2021/09/10/reader-center/author-ryan-mac/author-ryan-mac-thumbLarge.png)](https://www.nytimes.com/by/ryan-mac)

By [Ryan Mac](https://www.nytimes.com/by/ryan-mac)

Oct. 14, 2026 Updated 6:20 p.m. ET

[See more of our coverage in your search results.Encuentra más de nuestra cobertura en los resultados de búsqueda.Add The New York Times on Google Agrega The New York Times en Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?cs=0&hl=en&q=nytimes.com)

As it faces increased attacks from Russia and pressure from the White House, Ukrainian forces said on Tuesday that its battlefield operations had been hampered because they had lost some access to vital satellite-based communications.

For years, Ukraine’s armed forces have relied on SpaceX’s Starlink, which provides internet connectivity from satellites in lower earth orbit, and more recently its military-grade sister service, [Starshield](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/05/28/us/politics/elon-musk-space-launch-competition.html). Ukraine said on Tuesday that some military operations had been jeopardized, and specifically cited restrictions on Starshield.

“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” Serhiy Beskrestnov, who advises President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine on weapons technologies, wrote on [social media](https://t.me/serhii_flash/7807).

Mr. Beskrestnov said that the restrictions, which applied to devices traveling over 100 miles per hour and using Starshield, were related to “the current political situation.” Devices that broadcast satellite internet to users, which SpaceX calls “terminals,” can be placed on vehicles or drones to help guide them when traveling at high speeds.

Advertisement

[SKIP ADVERTISEMENT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/starshield-spacex-ukraine-starlink-satellites-musk.html#after-story-ad-1)

The Trump administration has been [pressuring Ukraine to limit its strikes on Russia](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/world/europe/trump-zelensky-diesel-energy-russia-.html), pushing Kyiv to stop attacking Russian oil refineries so more diesel can be pumped onto global markets. High fuel prices have stoked inflation and dented the prospects of President Trump’s Republican Party ahead of midterm elections next month.

Officials from Ukraine’s defense ministry placed the blame on SpaceX, saying it had unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals. They said the restriction complicates the operation of drone missions and reduces capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance and relaying signals.

items.title: OpenAI Engineer, Who Is Charged With Planting Bug, Advised Saudis
items.summary: The employee, now fired, had said he advised government agencies in Saudi Arabia. He was also listed as a partner at a venture firm with a Saudi prince.
items.full_text:
Title: OpenAI Engineer, Who Is Charged With Planting Bug, Advised Saudis - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/technology/openai-engineer-hidden-device-saudi-government.html

Published Time: Thu, 15 Oct 2026 02:28:44 GMT

Markdown Content:
The OpenAI engineer who was charged this week with [planting a secret recording device](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/technology/openai-worker-arrested-bugging.html) at the artificial intelligence company recently said he helped advise government agencies in Saudi Arabia on technology, and was listed as a partner at a venture capital firm alongside a member of the Saudi royal family.

In an Arabic [podcast interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u1Dq_g-d9XI) last month, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, said he and other Saudi tech professionals in Silicon Valley had formed a group that advised Saudi organizations, including the kingdom’s social insurance agency. Separately, RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm in Riyadh, the Saudi capital, lists Mr. Alfozan as a venture partner on its website, along with Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud.

Mr. Alfozan has a long history in Silicon Valley. He was an engineer at Meta before joining a start-up that went through Y Combinator, the Silicon Valley start-up accelerator. He gained permanent residency status in the United States in 2020, according to court documents, and was hired by OpenAI in July 2025.

Details about Mr. Alfozan are emerging after OpenAI disclosed on Tuesday that it had [discovered a hidden recording device](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/technology/openai-worker-arrested-bugging.html) in a conference room in one of its San Francisco buildings. The company said it had traced the device to Mr. Alfozan, who was arrested by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and charged with trying to secretly record conversations using an electronic device.

The incident has fueled concerns about the security of leading A.I. labs like OpenAI, which create advanced A.I. models that are among the most closely guarded secrets in the U.S. technology industry. Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, said that what had happened at OpenAI underscored how winning the A.I. race “is a national security prerogative.”

OpenAI said Mr. Alfozan did not appear to have inappropriately obtained or extracted sensitive information about its technology or customers. But the cloak-and-dagger details of the case have gained attention in Silicon Valley and in law enforcement and national security circles.

“Silicon Valley is ground zero for espionage from a variety of countries around the world,” said Amy Zegart, a professor at Stanford University who specializes in national security and intelligence. She added that she was “troubled” by the OpenAI incident and expected more cases “because these companies are so important.”

An OpenAI spokeswoman said the company had “a rigorous insider risk program to protect our employees, our intellectual property and customer data” and declined to discuss its monitoring process.

Mr. Alfozan did not respond to a request for comment. His lawyer, William Pernik, said his client was not charged with stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent, but did not respond to a request for comment regarding Mr. Alfozan’s Saudi ties.

RAED and the Saudi Embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment.

(The New York Times [sued](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/12/27/business/media/new-york-times-open-ai-microsoft-lawsuit.html) OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, accusing them of copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

In a filing in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, which was unsealed on Tuesday, prosecutors detailed how OpenAI’s security team had found a thumb-size recording device on Sept. 30, wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into the back of a television in an executive conference room. Only executives and their assistants could reserve the room, which was used for leadership meetings and briefings with government officials, the complaint said.

OpenAI employees then placed a camera in the conference room, prosecutors said, and it recorded Mr. Alfozan checking behind the TV on Oct. 5. That day, security staff found a second device in a bag that Mr. Alfozan had left in a printer room, the complaint said.

Last month, an A.I. chatbot account linked to Mr. Alfozan’s wife was used to ask how to build a continuous audio recorder, add Wi-Fi connectivity, encrypt its memory card and hide its activity, according to the complaint. Mr. Alfozan asked an A.I. tool to list meeting rooms in OpenAI’s offices and asked about locations for “leadership and exec,” prosecutors said.

Mr. Alfozan, his wife and another relative had booked one-way tickets to Saudi Arabia for this past Monday, prosecutors said in another court filing.

Born in Saudi Arabia’s central region of Qassim and raised in Dammam, Mr. Alfozan got into Mawhiba, the kingdom’s national program for gifted students, he said in the interview with “Identity Capital,” an Arabic podcast about professionals and careers. He later received a scholarship through a gifted-student program at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology and studied computer science and engineering at M.I.T.

On the podcast, Mr. Alfozan described meeting Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, then the deputy crown prince, during the prince’s 2016 visit to Silicon Valley. He said the prince had advised young Saudis in Silicon Valley to build their skills at the world’s leading companies and then bring that expertise home.

The company held an investor meeting on Wednesday as it plans a blockbuster initial public offering as soon as next month.

![Image 1: Dario Amodei holds a microphone and gestures while talking to Marc Benioff. A small audience watches from the right of the photo. ](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/13/multimedia/ANTHROPIC-INVESTORS-HFO-zgtc/ANTHROPIC-INVESTORS-HFO-zgtc-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, speaking to Marc Benioff, who runs Salesforce, last month in San Francisco.Credit...Manuel Orbegozo for The New York Times

Oct. 14, 2026 Updated 7:57 p.m. ET

Anthropic executives told a roomful of investors on Wednesday that the company’s revenue for the third quarter jumped about 45 percent from the prior quarter to $16.8 billion, as it pursues what may become the largest-ever initial public offering, two people with knowledge of the company’s presentation said.

The artificial intelligence giant, which makes the Claude chatbot, could aim to [raise more than $100 billion](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/21/technology/anthropic-ipo-100-billion.html) in a public listing, its bankers have said. That could value Anthropic at $2 trillion, pushing it past Elon Musk’s SpaceX — which [went public in June](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/11/technology/spacex-ipo-price.html) at a $1.77 trillion valuation — as the world’s biggest offering. The San Francisco company is expected to begin trading as early as next month.

In the meeting with potential investors at its headquarters, Anthropic sought to generate enthusiasm for the upcoming deal. Revenue was up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter. The company also said it was profitable after making certain adjustments, which is not a bottom-line number. And it said its gross margin, or revenue minus direct costs associated with generating that revenue, was 85 percent after making certain adjustments.

The Financial Times [earlier](https://www.ft.com/content/11632d03-358c-454b-af95-d06d4072932b?syn-25a6b1a6=1) reported details of Anthropic’s presentation.

Anthropic, which filed to go public in June, has not yet made its prospectus — which lays out its financial performance — public. Wednesday was the first official opportunity for potential I.P.O. investors to get a glimpse into the numbers, which may give insight into the health of the broader A.I. industry and will help determine the valuation Anthropic will get in its listing.

The I.P.O. is expected to be a milestone for Silicon Valley and Wall Street, even as Anthropic’s road to the public market has become increasingly difficult. Rising interest rates have [dampened the market](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/21/business/ai-data-center-ipos.html) for initial public offerings, while the company is grappling with questions about the sustainability of the A.I. industry’s increasingly debt-funded build-out.

A successful offering from Anthropic could reopen the door for other listings and provide a vote of confidence for the industry. A poorly received offering, on the other hand, could close the door on other listings and affect the broader stock market. Anthropic’s rival OpenAI has also filed to go public, probably next year.

Some of Anthropic’s bankers and backers argue that the company’s size, quick growth and potential opportunities distinguish it from others. Many of its investors, like Fidelity Investments and T. Rowe Price, are among the biggest investors in public offerings, so the company may have a built-in support base, bankers said.

Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, is embroiled in a major debate over A.I. safety. Last month, Dr. Amodei posted an essay [calling for a slowdown](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/12/technology/anthropic-dario-amodei-ai-slowdown.html) in the development of the most advanced A.I. technologies in order for proper guardrails to be installed.

His essay was followed by similar pushes from other industry leaders. President Trump later summoned executives to the White House and presented a [voluntary agreement](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117356435739432952) that they had signed to adopt safety policies that include risk reviews, auditing and evaluations of systems by third parties.

Some Anthropic investors have said they are keen to better understand how the company is defining “pacing” the development of these cutting-edge technologies. They are also focused on the potential impact of cheaper [open-weight](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/28/technology/open-weight-ai.html) A.I. models from China, which could steal some of Anthropic’s business.
